approachQuestion.prompt: A shipment has n indivisible parcels with positive integer weights. Each parcel may be selected at most once, and different parcels may have equal weights. Return whether some subset has total weight exactly T. Choosing no parcels is allowed. Examples: weights=[3,5,5], T=10 → true; weights=[3,5], T=6 → false; weights=[7], T=0 → true. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: Input is read-only. Return only a Boolean, not selected parcel indices.

options.text: Initialize reachable[0]=true and all other entries through T to false. For each weight w, visit s from T down to w and set reachable[s] to reachable[s] OR reachable[s−w]. Return reachable[T].
options.feedback: Descending sums read values from before this parcel was considered. A parcel cannot create a smaller sum and then reuse that new sum during the same pass.

options.text: Keep a Boolean table for every prefix of parcels and every sum through T. Each row either omits its last parcel or adds it to a reachable sum from the preceding row.
options.feedback: This is correct even for duplicate weights, because each row represents one parcel. Keeping all prefix rows adds removable storage: only the preceding row is read, and descending updates can reuse one array.

options.text: Initialize the same array, but for each weight w update sums from w upward through T, using reachable[s−w] from the current array.
options.feedback: This can reuse a parcel. With weights=[3,5], T=6, the first pass sets reachable[3] and then reachable[6], although only one parcel weighs 3.

options.text: Return true exactly when the sum of all parcel weights is at least T.
options.feedback: Having enough total weight does not imply an exact subset. Weights=[4,7], T=5 has total 11 but no subset totaling 5.

feedback.reason: Choose an update order that preserves the previous-item state and prevents accidental unlimited reuse.
details: Track which exact sums are reachable. Start with sum zero. Process one parcel at a time, updating sums downward so every source entry still describes choices made before that parcel.

Descending sums keep each predecessor state from before the current parcel. Ascending sums could reuse that parcel repeatedly. Reachability is Boolean: distinct ways to reach one sum do not create a larger reachable amount.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze descending-reachability with n parcels: allocate and initialize all T+1 Boolean entries, then scan each parcel and update sums downward from T to its weight when that weight is at most T. Do not stop early. Use a word per Boolean, not a packed bitset. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Treat n and T as independent variable parameters. Include initialization and the T=0 and n=0 cases.

Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.

feedback.reason: Include table initialization and all parcel-by-sum transitions, including zero-parameter cases.
details: Initializing the array takes T+1 work, scanning weights takes n work, and updates take up to nT work. With small weights the worst case attains these costs. Together they are tightly bounded by (n+1)(T+1), including zero parameters. The only growing allocation contains T+1 entries.
“O(n+T+1) time, O(T+1) auxiliary space”: One parcel may update nearly every sum; adding the two dimensions omits their repeated work.
“O((n+1)(T+1)) time, O(n(T+1)+1) auxiliary space”: Only a single sum array is retained; no row is stored for each parcel.
“O((n+1)(T+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Even with downward updates, the method retains T+1 Boolean entries.
